blocks.content: A thread inside a lock sometimes needs to wait for a specific condition to become true before it can safely continue. Condition variables are the tool that makes that waiting both correct and efficient.
1. The Problem They Solve

Imagine a consumer thread that needs the shared buffer to have at least one item before it can proceed. It cannot just hold the lock and loop, checking the buffer over and over, because holding the lock while busy looping blocks every other thread, including the producer thread that could actually add an item and make the condition true.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408559628-775964503.png
Condition variables solve this by letting a thread give up the lock while it waits, so other threads can make progress, and get woken up automatically once the condition might have changed.
2. wait(): Release and Sleep, Atomically
Calling wait() on a condition variable does two things in a single, indivisible step: it releases the lock the thread is currently holding, and it puts the thread to sleep.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408559628-871135755.png

This atomicity is not a minor implementation detail, it is essential for correctness. If releasing the lock and going to sleep were two separate steps, another thread could sneak in during the tiny gap between them, change the condition, and signal, and the first thread would miss that wakeup entirely because it had not started sleeping yet.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408560072-261148138.png
3. signal(): Wake One Thread

signal(), sometimes called notify(), wakes up exactly one thread waiting on the condition variable. That thread does not resume running immediately though, it must first reacquire the lock, and it may have to wait in line behind whoever currently holds it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408560073-225066500.png
4. notify_all() / broadcast(): Wake Everyone

Sometimes more than one waiting thread could independently proceed once a condition changes. notify_all() wakes every thread waiting on the condition variable at once, and they all then compete to reacquire the lock one at a time.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408560073-817685326.png
5. The Critical Rule: Check in a Loop, Not an If
blocks.text: 5. The Critical Rule: Check in a Loop, Not an If

blocks.content: A woken thread must recheck the actual condition in a while loop, never assume it is true just because it woke up. Spurious wakeups can happen, where a thread wakes with no real signal at all due to implementation details.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408560074-371125903.png
blocks.alt: The Critical Rule: Check in a Loop, Not an If

blocks.content: Even a genuine signal does not guarantee the condition is STILL true by the time this particular thread finally reacquires the lock, since a faster competing thread might have already consumed it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408560074-249168717.png
blocks.alt: The Critical Rule: Check in a Loop, Not an If

blocks.title: The single most common bug here
blocks.content: Using an if check instead of a while loop before wait() is the classic condition variable mistake. Always use a loop.
6. Worked Example: Bounded Buffer

A producer thread waits on a not full condition before adding an item, then signals not empty. A consumer thread waits on a not empty condition before removing an item, then signals not full. Both operate inside the same lock.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408560075-468326818.png
7. Common Mistakes

["Using if instead of while to check the condition after waking, missing both spurious wakeups and races with faster competing threads.","Forgetting that a signaled thread does not get the lock automatically, it still has to compete to reacquire it."]
items: Using if instead of while to check the condition after waking, missing both spurious wakeups and races with faster competing threads.
Forgetting that a signaled thread does not get the lock automatically, it still has to compete to reacquire it.

blocks.content: 8. Interview Angle

The if versus while distinction is one of the sharpest, most common interview checks on this topic. Being able to explain exactly why while is required, not just that it is the convention, is what demonstrates real understanding.
